prs.title: ZIP 374: Align the bundle anchor requirements with ZIP 225
prs.author: briandevans

 For a PCZT whose `tx_version` is 5:
 
-- Every shielded bundle anchor MUST be set at the time the bundle's first

prs.title: Add draft ZIP: FROST Member Backup Strings for Shielded Zcash
prs.author: KHADEVS

@@ -0,0 +1,537 @@
+    ZIP: Unassigned
+    Title: FROST Member Backup Strings for Shielded Zcash
+    Owners: Khadim <openpgp-wallet@protonmail.com>
+            aryaethn <aryaethn@gmail.com>
+    Credits: Hanh (hhanh00), for the zkfrost string in Zkool
+    Status: Draft
+    Category: Wallet
+    Created: 2026-10-26
+    License: MIT
+    Discussions-To: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/issues/1413>
+    Pull-Request: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1432>
+
+
+# Terminology
+
+The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "SHOULD", and "SHOULD NOT" in this document
+are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [^BCP14] when, and only when,
+they appear in all capitals.
+
+The terms "Mainnet" and "Testnet" in this document are to be interpreted as
+defined in the Zcash protocol specification [^protocol-networks].
+
+The terms below are to be interpreted as follows:
+
+Group
+
+: A set of $n$ participants holding a FROST threshold key for Orchard-protocol
+  spend authorization [^zip-0312], any $t$ of whom can sign.
+
+Member
+
+: One participant of a group, identified by its FROST identifier.
+
+Signing share
+
+: The member's secret share of the group's Spend authorizing key, as output
+  by key generation.
+
+Group verifying key, $\mathsf{ak}$
+
+: The FROST group public key, used as the Spend validating key
+  $\mathsf{ak}$ of the group's Orchard full viewing key. Its encoding has a
+  $\tilde{y}$ bit of $0$, as § 4.2.3 of the protocol specification requires
+  [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents].
+
+$\mathsf{sk}$
+
+: The 32-byte value the members agree on during key generation, from which
+  $\mathsf{nk}$, $\mathsf{rivk}$ and, under ZIP 2005, $\mathsf{qsk}$ and
+  $\mathsf{qk}$ are derived [^zip-2005-usagewithfrost].
+
+Derivation
+
+: How $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ are obtained from $\mathsf{sk}$ and
+  $\mathsf{ak}$. This ZIP knows two, defined in [Derivations].
+
+Member backup string
+
+: The string defined in this ZIP.
+
+
+# Abstract
+
+This ZIP defines a backup string for one member of a FROST group that spends
+shielded ZEC with Orchard-protocol keys (in the Orchard or Ironwood pool). The
+string holds the member's identifier, the threshold, the group size, the
+member's signing share and the group's $\mathsf{sk}$. Together with the group's
+unified full viewing key, it is enough to rebuild the member in any wallet that
+implements this ZIP, without the other members being online. Restoring checks
+the string against the viewing key, which both detects a string from another
+group and tells the wallet which key derivation the group uses.
+
+Version 1 of the payload is byte-for-byte the `zkfrost` string that Zkool
+already ships, so existing backups stay valid.
+
+The string is more sensitive than the signing share it carries: it also
+carries $\mathsf{sk}$, from which a holder can compute the group's quantum
+spending key $\mathsf{qsk}$ [^zip-2005]. It never appears on chain.
+
+
+# Motivation
+
+Several wallets now offer FROST groups for shielded ZEC: Zkool, Zafe,
+Konclave, and the Zcash Foundation's tools. Each one backs up its members in its
+own format, so a member can only restore their seat in the app that created
+it. In July 2026, Zkool's author described the situation: "There is no
+standard for it. I choose a way that makes it restorable on Zkool only. One
+day, someone will write a ZIP." [^zkool-forum]
+
+Since then, Zkool has moved to a minimal backup string (`zkfrost`, Zkool
+6.35.0) that holds only what a member needs. This ZIP takes that string as its
+first version, so that:
+
+- a user can move a seat from one wallet to another, or restore it in a
+  different app after losing a device;
+- a group can mix implementations, which avoids having every signer come from
+  one vendor;
+- funds stay reachable if one app is abandoned.
+
+ZIP 2005 adds a reason. To recover notes with the Recovery Protocol, "it is
+necessary to retain, or be able to rederive, $\mathsf{sk}$, and also to know
+whether $\mathsf{use\_qsk}$ was used to derive the $\mathsf{ivk}$ and
+addresses" [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]. A backup format is where
+that knowledge has to live.
+
+
+# Privacy Implications
+
+The string never leaves the member's custody in normal use and is not
+published on chain, so this ZIP changes nothing for on-chain privacy.
+
+Combined with the group's unified full viewing key, a string gives no viewing
+capability beyond what that viewing key already gives. Without the viewing
+key, $\mathsf{sk}$ yields $\mathsf{nk}$ but not the incoming viewing key, which
+also depends on $\mathsf{ak}$. The string does reveal $t$, $n$ and the member's
+identifier.
+
+A wallet that shows the string as a QR code exposes it to cameras and
+onlookers, as with any secret displayed on screen.
+
+
+# Requirements
+
+- A member can be rebuilt from its string and the group's unified full viewing
+  key, with no other member online.
+- A wallet detects a string that belongs to another group before using it.
+- The restore tells which derivation the group uses.
+- The format does not depend on how $\mathsf{sk}$ was agreed.
+- Backups made with Zkool's `zkfrost` string stay valid.
+- The format can gain new versions without breaking existing strings.
+
+
+# Non-requirements
+
+- Key generation, including how the members agree on $\mathsf{sk}$
+  [^zip-0312-key-generation].
+- Signing, and the transport between members.
+- Encryption of the string at rest (see [Open issues]).
+- A birthday height. ZIP 316 lets a unified full viewing key carry one
+  (typecode $\mathtt{0xC0}$) [^zip-0316-birthday], and the restore already
+  needs that key.
+- Splitting $\mathsf{qsk}$ between members.
+- FROST groups using Sapling keys.
+
+
+# Specification
+
+## Derivations
+
+Let $\mathsf{H^{ask}}$, $\mathsf{H^{nk}}$, $\mathsf{H^{rivk}}$,
+$\mathsf{H^{qsk}}$, $\mathsf{H^{qk}}$ and
+$\mathsf{H}^{\mathsf{rivk\_ext}}_{\mathsf{qk}}$ be as defined in § 4.2.3
+of the protocol specification as updated by ZIP 2005
+[^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents].
+
+ZIP 2005 derivation
+
+: $\mathsf{nk} = \mathsf{H^{nk}}(\mathsf{sk})$, and
+  $\mathsf{rivk} = \mathsf{H}^{\mathsf{rivk\_ext}}_{\mathsf{qk}}(\mathsf{ak}, \mathsf{nk})$
+  where $\mathsf{qk} = \mathsf{H^{qk}}(\mathsf{H^{qsk}}(\mathsf{sk}))$. This is
+  the $\mathsf{use\_qsk} = \mathsf{true}$ branch that ZIP 2005 requires for
+  FROST [^zip-2005-usagewithfrost]. Notes received by such a group are
+  quantum recoverable.
+
+Legacy derivation
+
+: $\mathsf{nk} = \mathsf{H^{nk}}(\mathsf{sk})$ and
+  $\mathsf{rivk} = \mathsf{H^{rivk}}(\mathsf{sk})$, with the group verifying key
+  as $\mathsf{ak}$. Zkool created groups this way before supporting ZIP 2005.
+  Such a group follows neither branch of § 4.2.3
+  [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]: $\mathsf{ak}$ is not derived from
+  $\mathsf{sk}$, and $\mathsf{rivk}$ does not commit to a $\mathsf{qk}$. Notes
+  received by such a group are therefore not quantum recoverable.
+
+## Encoding
+
+A member backup string is the Bech32m [^bip-0350] encoding of a payload, with
+the human-readable part `zkfrost`. As in ZIP 316 [^zip-0316], the length limit
+of Bech32m is not applied; a version 1 string is 123 characters long.
+
+Encoders MUST produce lowercase strings. Decoders MUST accept a string that is
+entirely lowercase or entirely uppercase, and MUST reject a string in mixed
+case, as Bech32m requires. A wallet can still show the string in uppercase,
+for instance in a QR code (see [Rationale]), by converting it after encoding.
+
+The human-readable part is the same on Mainnet and Testnet, and the payload
+names no network: the network is given by the unified full viewing key used to
+restore. A string paired with another group's viewing key, on either network,
+fails the check in [Restore].
+
+## Payload, version 1
+
+| Offset | Size | Field |
+|--------|------|-------|
+| 0      | 1    | format version, $\mathtt{0x01}$ |
+| 1      | 1    | member identifier $i$ |
+| 2      | 1    | threshold $t$ |
+| 3      | 1    | group size $n$ |
+| 4      | 32   | signing share |
+| 36     | 32   | $\mathsf{sk}$ |
+
+The member's FROST identifier is the Pallas scalar with integer value $i$.
+The group size $n$ is the number of members.
+
+The signing share is the little-endian encoding of a Pallas scalar, as in the
+FROST(Pallas, BLAKE2b-512) ciphersuite [^zip-0312]. It MUST be the share that
+matches the $\mathsf{ak}$ in the group's viewing key. Key generation can output
+a group key with either $\tilde{y}$ bit; when it is $1$, the group key and
+every share are negated. The `reddsa` crate does this at the end of its key
+generation, and frost-client does it after the DKG. An implementation that
+skips this step would export a wrong share for about half of all groups.
+
+## Decoding
+
+A decoder MUST reject the string if any of the following holds:
+
+- it is not valid Bech32m, including a bad checksum, a Bech32 checksum, or
+  mixed case;
+- the bits left over when converting its data part to bytes are more than 4
+  or not all zero, as ZIP 173 requires [^zip-0173]. A version 1 string leaves
+  1 bit, so each payload has only one lowercase string;
+- its human-readable part, compared case-insensitively, is not `zkfrost`;
+- the format version is not $\mathtt{0x01}$;
+- the payload is not exactly 68 bytes long;
+- $n = 0$, $i = 0$, $i > n$, $t < 2$, or $t > n$. FROST needs at least two
+  signers.
+
+Checking the version before the length lets a decoder report a string of a
+later version as unsupported rather than as corrupt.
+
+## Restore
+
+The inputs are a member backup string and the group's unified full viewing
+key. The viewing key MUST contain an Orchard component (typecode
+$\mathtt{0x03}$ [^zip-0316]), which holds $\mathsf{ak}$, $\mathsf{nk}$ and
+$\mathsf{rivk}$. Ironwood uses the same Orchard-protocol keys.
+
+1. Decode the string as above.
+2. Reject the string if $\mathsf{sk}$ is not a valid Orchard spending key,
+   that is if $\mathsf{H^{ask}}(\mathsf{sk}) = 0$, or if the signing share is
+   not the canonical encoding of a Pallas scalar, or is zero. (A group's
+   $\mathsf{ask}$ is not derived from $\mathsf{sk}$; the first check only keeps
+   decoders in agreement with the validity rule for Orchard spending keys. The
+   verifying share of a zero share is the identity, which ZIP 312 does not
+   allow [^zip-0312].)
+3. Take $\mathsf{ak}$ from the viewing key. Compute $\mathsf{nk}$ and
+   $\mathsf{rivk}$ under each derivation of [Derivations].
+4. If the ZIP 2005 derivation gives the viewing key's $\mathsf{nk}$ and
+   $\mathsf{rivk}$, the group follows the ZIP 2005 derivation. Otherwise, if
+   the legacy derivation does, the group follows the legacy derivation.
+   Otherwise the wallet MUST reject the string: it belongs to another group.
+5. Rebuild the member's key material from the identifier, the signing share,
+   the threshold $t$ and $\mathsf{ak}$ as the group verifying key. If the
+   wallet knows the group's verifying shares, it SHOULD check that the
+   member's verifying share matches.
+
+A wallet SHOULD tell the user which derivation was found, and SHOULD warn when
+it is the legacy one, whose notes are not quantum recoverable.
+
+The check in step 4 proves that the viewing key was derived from the string's
+$\mathsf{sk}$, not that its $\mathsf{ak}$ is the group's (see
+[Security Considerations]). Before it shows an address to receive funds, a
+wallet SHOULD check the viewing key against a source the member trusts, such as
+the export made with its own string (see [Export]), an address of the group
+that the member recorded before and that the viewing key gives, or the same
+viewing key obtained from at least two other members. A member that lost its
+device may have lost its export too, and then has to ask the others for the
+key, which is the case the attack needs: if one of the members it asks is
+honest, a forged key shows up as a mismatch.
+
+After the restore, the wallet MUST retain $\mathsf{sk}$ when the group follows
+the ZIP 2005 derivation. ZIP 2005 makes $\mathsf{qsk}$, which is derived from
+$\mathsf{sk}$, essential for recovering the group's notes once the current
+Orchard protocol is disabled [^zip-2005-usagewithfrost], and the signing
+share and viewing key alone do not give it. A wallet SHOULD also retain
+$\mathsf{sk}$ for a legacy group, since without it the member cannot export
+its string again.
+
+A restored member holds no signing nonces. It MUST generate fresh ones for its
+next signing session.
+
+The check in step 4 proves $\mathsf{sk}$, not the signing share. A wrong share,
+such as one stored with the wrong sign, passes the restore and is caught at the
+member's first signing: the verifying shares of the $t$ signers, which travel
+with their commitments, interpolate to $\mathsf{ak}$ only if every one of them
+is right. The signing transport is out of scope for this ZIP, but a signing
+protocol used with these strings SHOULD carry each signer's verifying share,
+so that a member restored from a string is checked when it first signs.
+
+## Export
+
+A wallet that exports a member backup string SHOULD export the group's unified
+full viewing key with it, or tell the user that the restore needs it. ZIP 2005
+asks FROST members to retain the group verifying key $\mathsf{ak}$
+[^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]; in version 1 it is only held by the
+viewing key.
+
+A wallet MUST NOT put signing nonces, or any other secret beyond the fields
+above, in a version 1 string.
+
+## Storage and transmission
+
+Wallets MUST protect every member backup string at least as securely and
+reliably as $\mathsf{ask}$, as ZIP 2005 requires of $\mathsf{qsk}$
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost], and not merely like one signing share.
+
+Wallets SHOULD NOT store or transmit a string encrypted only under public-key
+encryption based on discrete logarithms or on factoring, such as Orchard note
+encryption, X25519, or RSA and elliptic-curve OpenPGP keys.
+
+
+# Rationale
+
+**Bech32m.** It gives a checksum that catches copy errors and a string users
+can paste or show as a QR code. An uppercase string fits the QR alphanumeric
+mode, which makes the code smaller. Its checksum guarantees the detection of
+any error affecting at most 4 characters only for strings of at most 90
+characters [^zip-0173] [^bip-0350]. A version 1 string is 123 characters
+long, so it keeps the 30-bit checksum without that guarantee, as unified
+addresses and viewing keys do [^zip-0316].
+
+**No network in the string.** A member's share is the same on every network
+the group lives on. The viewing key carries the network.
+
+**$\mathsf{ak}$ is not stored.** The restore needs the viewing key anyway to
+scan the chain, and checking $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ against it
+catches a string from another group. The cost is that the string does not
+authenticate $\mathsf{ak}$ (see [Security Considerations]).
+
+**$\mathsf{sk}$ is stored whole.** ZIP 2005 makes it necessary "to retain, or
+be able to rederive, $\mathsf{sk}$" [^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents],
+and every member already holds it, along with $\mathsf{qsk}$
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost].
+
+**The derivation is found, not recorded.** Version 1 is Zkool's existing
+payload, which has no field for it. With two derivations and the viewing key at
+hand, trying both is cheap and unambiguous: both matching would need a
+collision in the hash functions behind $\mathsf{rivk}$. A later version can
+record the derivation explicitly (see [Open issues]).
+
+**One-byte identifier.** It covers groups whose identifiers are the integers
+1 to $n$, as in Zkool and in frost-client's trusted-dealer key generation.
+frost-client's DKG and Zafe derive 32-byte identifiers, which need another
+version (see [Open issues]).
+
+**Version 1 is Zkool's payload.** Backups users already made keep working,
+and the first implementation exists today.
+
+
+# Security Considerations
+
+A string holds one signing share. Fewer than $t$ strings cannot spend, as long
+as discrete logarithms on the Pallas curve stay hard.
+
+Every string also holds $\mathsf{sk}$, which yields $\mathsf{qsk}$. ZIP 2005
+notes that "a quantum adversary may be able to steal the funds with only
+access to $\mathsf{qsk}$, which is held by every participant"
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost]. Against such an adversary the threshold may give no
+protection: one leaked string, from any member, may be enough to steal the
+funds. ZIP 2005 requires each participant to "treat $\mathsf{qsk}$ as a
+secret held at least as securely and reliably as $\mathsf{ask}$"
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost], which is why [Storage and transmission] asks the
+same for every string.
+
+For the same reason, a string that is stored or sent encrypted only under
+public-key encryption based on discrete logarithms or on factoring is exposed
+to an adversary who records the ciphertext now and gains a quantum computer
+later. A passphrase with a memory-hard KDF and an AEAD (see [Open issues])
+does not have this weakness.
+
+The restore does not prove the signing share (see [Restore]). A wrong share,
+for instance one exported with the wrong sign (see [Payload, version 1]),
+gives signature shares that fail verification. It stops that member from
+signing until it is restored from a correct string, but it cannot sign
+anything or leak the other shares.
+
+The restore does not authenticate $\mathsf{ak}$ either. Every member holds
+$\mathsf{sk}$, so a dishonest member can build a viewing key around another
+$\mathsf{ak}$, for instance one whose secret it holds alone, with the
+$\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ that either derivation gives for it. A string
+restored with that key passes every check in [Restore], and the wallet then
+shows addresses that only that member can spend from. The wallet would not see
+the group's notes, and the group's signatures would not verify under that
+$\mathsf{ak}$, but funds received at those addresses before anyone notices are
+lost to the group. Checking the viewing key against a trusted source, as
+[Restore] asks, prevents this; so would carrying $\mathsf{ak}$ in the string
+(see [Open issues]).
+
+A member restored from a string has the same authority as before: the string
+adds no signer to the group. It carries no nonces, so a restore cannot bring
+back a nonce that was already used or published.
+
+
+# Deployment
+
+This ZIP changes no consensus rule. Wallets can adopt it at any time.
+
+
+# Reference implementation
+
+- Zkool: `rust/src/frost/backup.rs` in hhanh00/zkool2, released in Zkool
+  6.35.0 [^zkool-backup].
+- frost-zec: `src/backup.rs` in OpenPGP-Wallet/frost-zec, by one of this
+  ZIP's owners, written from this ZIP's rules apart from Zkool's code, with
+  `backup export` and `backup restore` commands [^frost-zec-backup].
+
+
+# Test vectors
+
+The test vectors are generated by the Python code proposed in
+zcash/zcash-test-vectors#136 [^zcash-test-vectors-pr], in three files:
+`frost_member_backup`, `frost_member_backup_decoding` and
+`frost_member_backup_restore`.
+They cover a 2-of-3 ZIP 2005 group, a 2-of-3 legacy group together with the
+ZIP 2005 viewing key built from the same $\mathsf{sk}$ and $\mathsf{ak}$ (whose
+strings restore under either key, with a different derivation), and a 3-of-5
+ZIP 2005 group; an uppercase string; seventeen strings that decoders must
+reject, two of them for the padding rule and one with a threshold of 1; and
+four cases that decode but that the restore must reject: a valid string
+paired with another group's viewing key, a string whose signing share is not
+canonical, one whose signing share is zero, and a viewing key with no Orchard
+component.
+
+Every valid string decodes to the same fields and matches the stated
+derivation with Zkool's code, and every $t$-subset of members restored from
+their strings produces a FROST signature that verifies under $\mathsf{ak}$.
+Zkool 6.35.0 rejects every invalid string except three. It does not check
+the padding bits, and decodes the two padding strings to the same fields as
+the valid string they come from; it also accepts a threshold of 1. Zkool
+6.36.0 rejects all three: it has the padding fix, hhanh00/zkool2#1468
+[^zkool-padding-fix], and its decoder now refuses a threshold below 2.
+A third decoder, by the other owner of this ZIP, with the derivations written
+directly from BIP 350, ZIP 316 and ZIP 2005 and no Zcash library, gives the
+expected result for every string, both viewing keys of each group, and every
+rejected case but the share of zero, added since. With frost-client's version
+of `reddsa`, every $t$-subset also rebuilds $\mathsf{ak}$ and signs.
+
+One member of the 2-of-3 ZIP 2005 group (byte strings in hex):
+
+    sk      24cf13c724758886048e05834d5d0a644e9c8e155d7e0bac3f25586b6caa11c3
+    ak      a0dffa5f21db1b2c6cc72d9b6af9d777884c2c7d3e06ad479732bec46cee110d
+    nk      e32868e0d0770d63ad17b8a807c8133bfb957c81fb973f1c43531c7cc15e5831
+    qsk     7193049fb014e408fd139cfcc47c58d6c20451473bab44ccb9fffc983ecf8ada
+    qk      eec37a6202cd2f8b1bea8279bf87ef0dcb2bf73bbec28f077c4c5e1a743dd79f
+    rivk    d0971e49314b6ad96d67af2766afc7db08fe6bf01f3ab0d84376016aad6ef419
+    t, n    2, 3
+    id      1
+    share   2caaa5adfcad8ac0bb8c50dcdbbc1e954825be403f97f44bc1d6c543e15d4f3b
+    string  zkfrost1qyqsyqev42j6ml9d3tqthrzsmndmc854fqjmuspljl6yhswkc4p7zh208vjv7y78y36c3psy3czcxn2apfjya8ywz4whuzav8uj4s6mv4gguxm4ktp7
+    ufvk    uview1mvknnjr2s9cuc7z5kjsd3twesswde37tpfw2z4v5a8jmsnwdwsg8sc2hdq302ud7j57d7dvmmt6mtc6c3fk7zkdyx5mrhq8fvyw8xp0dlgzl8kkwawt9j7m9z5adwpuskfscg5fyrpc0sca8lydtxfw7hfaaydtg88ayqj6y89a9jllhupn3hzgp7vq6d
+
+
+# Open issues
+
+- **Identifier encoding.** frost-client's DKG derives identifiers as
+  `Identifier::derive(session_id || pubkey)`, and Zafe from the vault id and
+  the member's identity key, so groups created by either use full 32-byte
+  identifiers (frost-client's trusted dealer uses 1 to $n$). For their groups
+  to fit, a version 2 needs a type byte followed by a short or a full
+  identifier.
+- **Identifiers after a refresh.** Refreshing shares to remove a member keeps
+  the other members' identifiers [^frost-refresh], so a group can end up with
+  identifiers 1, 2 and 4 and $n = 3$. Version 1 rejects member 4 ($i > n$), so
+  it covers only groups whose identifiers are 1 to $n$, which is what Zkool
+  creates. A version 2 could drop that check: the restore can match the
+  identifier against the group's verifying shares when it knows them.
+- **Explicit derivation.** A version 2 could record the derivation, so a
+  restore does not depend on trying each one, and a third derivation could be
+  added without ambiguity.
+- **Groups with no $\mathsf{sk}$.** zcash-sign's `generate`, which Konclave
+  uses, derives $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ from a random $\mathsf{sk}$
+  and then discards it, so version 1 cannot hold its groups. A version 2 could
+  record that $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ come from the viewing key,
+  leave $\mathsf{sk}$ out, and carry the viewing key itself (next item).
+  Carrying only $\mathsf{ak}$, as first suggested in zcash/zips#1413, would let
+  the restore catch a viewing key from another group, but not a different
+  viewing key for the same group. Such groups are not quantum recoverable
+  under ZIP 2005.
+- **The viewing key in the string**, so that a restore needs only the string.
+  For a group with no $\mathsf{sk}$, the viewing key is the only source of
+  $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$. A version 2 would carry the raw 96-byte
+  Orchard full viewing key rather than its unified encoding, so that the
+  string stays network-agnostic. With the viewing key in the string, nothing
+  outside it is left to mismatch. For a group with $\mathsf{sk}$,
+  $\mathsf{ak}$ is enough, since $\mathsf{nk}$ and $\mathsf{rivk}$ follow from
+  $\mathsf{sk}$ and $\mathsf{ak}$. Either way, $\mathsf{ak}$ would then come
+  from the member's own backup rather than from a viewing key obtained
+  elsewhere (see [Security Considerations]). A string for a group with no
+  $\mathsf{sk}$ would be about 230 characters long, or 280 with a 32-byte
+  identifier (see [Rationale] on Bech32m).
+- **Birthday height in version 2.** A raw Orchard full viewing key does not
+  carry the birthday height that ZIP 316 allows in the unified encoding
+  [^zip-0316-birthday], so a string that restores on its own would need a
+  birthday field of its own, as Konclave noted in zcash/zips#1413. A height
+  only means something on one network, so the field would either name the
+  network or apply to the network the wallet restores on.
+- **Passphrase profile.** An optional version encrypting the payload with a
+  memory-hard KDF and an AEAD, as Zafe does for its backups.
+- **Human-readable part.** `zkfrost` is kept for compatibility with existing
+  backups. Should a later version use a more neutral one?
+
+
+# References
+
+[^BCP14]: [Information on BCP 14 — "RFC 2119: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels" and "RFC 8174: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words"](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/bcp14)
+
+[^protocol-networks]: [Zcash Protocol Specification, Version 2026.8.0 [NU6.3]. Section 3.12: Mainnet and Testnet](protocol/protocol.pdf#networks)
+
+[^protocol-updated-orchardkeycomponents]: [Zcash Protocol Specification, Version 2026.8.0 [NU6.3]. Section 4.2.3: Orchard Key Components](protocol/protocol.pdf#orchardkeycomponents)
+
+[^zip-0173]: [ZIP 173: Bech32 Format](zip-0173.rst)
+
+[^zip-0312]: [ZIP 312: FROST for Spend Authorization Multisignatures](zip-0312.rst)
+
+[^zip-0312-key-generation]: [ZIP 312: FROST for Spend Authorization Multisignatures — Key Generation](zip-0312.rst#key-generation)
+
+[^zip-0316]: [ZIP 316: Unified Addresses and Unified Viewing Keys](zip-0316.rst)
+
+[^zip-2005]: [ZIP 2005: Ironwood Quantum Recoverability](zip-2005.md)
+
+[^zip-2005-usagewithfrost]: [ZIP 2005: Ironwood Quantum Recoverability — Usage with FROST](zip-2005.md#usagewithfrost)
+
+[^bip-0350]: [BIP 350: Bech32m format for v1+ witness addresses](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0350.mediawiki)

prs.title: Add draft ZIP: Wallet-to-Wallet Messaging
prs.author: arya2
prs.bodyExcerpt: Adds `zips/draft-arya-wallet-to-wallet-messaging.md`, a Standards / Wallet draft specifying an off-chain channel between wallets: a wallet that holds another wallet's Unified Address deposits an encrypted Envelope in a Mailbox over an anonymity network, and the recipient fetches it later. The second

files.patch:
@@ -0,0 +1,558 @@
+    ZIP: Unassigned
+    Title: Wallet-to-Wallet Messaging
+    Owners: Arya <arya@zfnd.org>
+            Ying Tong Lai <yingtong.lai@gmail.com>
+    Status: Draft
+    Category: Standards / Wallet
+    Created: 2026-11-03
+    License: MIT
+    Pull-Request: <https://github.com/zcash/zips/pull/1435>
+
+
+# Terminology
+
+The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", and "MAY" in this
+document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [^BCP14] when, and only
+when, they appear in all capitals.
+
+The terms "Unified Address" and "Receiver" are to be interpreted as defined
+in ZIP 316. [^zip-0316]
+
+Envelope
+
+: An encrypted message, padded to one of three sizes.
+
+Mailbox
+
+: A queue of Envelopes held by a Mailbox Server under a Mailbox ID.
+
+Conversation
+
+: The state two wallets share after a first Envelope: a secret from which
+  they derive Envelope keys and Mailbox IDs.
+
+Contact Mailbox, Pairwise Mailbox
+
+: The Mailbox derived from an Orchard Receiver, and one derived from a
+  Conversation, a direction, and a week-long epoch.
+
+Routing Binding
+
+: A specification of how wallets reach Mailbox Servers, and optionally each
+  other, over one anonymity network.
+
+
+# Abstract
+
+This ZIP specifies an off-chain channel between Zcash wallets. A wallet that
+holds another wallet's Unified Address deposits an encrypted Envelope in a
+Mailbox, reaching the Mailbox Server over an anonymity network, and the
+recipient fetches it later. Neither wallet reveals its network identity to
+the other or to the server.
+
+Nothing is added to the Unified Address. The Mailbox ID and Mailbox Server
+are derived from the address's Orchard Receiver, the Envelope is encrypted to
+that Receiver using the Orchard key agreement, and fetching requires the
+incoming viewing key. Every first Envelope also starts a Conversation, whose
+mailboxes rotate each epoch, so that an ongoing exchange does not accumulate
+metadata under one identifier. Routing is separate from storage: mailboxes
+are reached over any supported anonymity network, and prompt replies can also
+go directly between the wallets. Payload types are defined for
+acknowledgements, text, ZIP 321 payment requests, and PCZTs.
+
+Anyone who holds the recipient's Orchard incoming viewing key can read and
+fetch its Envelopes, and a Mailbox Server sees the volume and timing of what
+each Mailbox ID receives. Appendix A sketches Routing Bindings for the Nym
+mixnet [^nym] and for Tor. [^tor-rend]
+
+
+# Motivation
+
+Several wallet protocols need a direct channel between wallets, and each
+wallet that wants one currently builds its own:
+
+- Multisig and hardware-signer flows pass PCZTs [^pczt] between parties.
+- FROST signing (ZIP 312 [^zip-0312]) needs a confidential, authenticated
+  channel that ZIP 312 leaves out of scope. This ZIP supplies confidentiality
+  and anonymity; a FROST payload would carry its own authentication.
+- Payment requests (ZIP 321 [^zip-0321]) have no wallet-to-wallet transport.
+- Project Tachyon [^tachyon] [^tachyon-post] proposes removing in-band secret
+  distribution from transactions, which makes an off-chain delivery channel a
+  requirement.
+
+On-chain memos are the only standard channel today. Even without their size
+cap (ZIP 231 [^zip-0231]) they cost fees, are stored forever, and need a
+block confirmation per round. ZIP 324 [^zip-0324] covers the case where the
+sender has no address for the recipient; this ZIP covers the case where it
+does.
+
+Out-of-band delivery over a mixnet, with a mailbox for offline recipients,
+has been proposed before. [^hornby-2020] [^zips-629] The Nym × Zcash
+integration [^nym-zcash] routes chain-sync and transaction submission through
+the mixnet, not wallet-to-wallet messages.
+
+
+# Privacy Implications
+
+**Incoming viewing key holders.** Whoever holds an account's Orchard incoming
+viewing key can read and fetch every Envelope ever sent to its addresses, and
+by fetching can cause the server to delete them. It can also derive the
+secret of every Conversation started with those addresses, and so read,
+fetch, and send Envelopes in them, in both directions. There is no forward
+secrecy. Envelopes can reveal more than notes do: a PCZT shows a transaction
+before it is signed. The viewing keys of the wallet that starts a
+Conversation give no access to it.
+
+All diversified addresses of an account share one incoming viewing key, so
+using a different address does not help. Viewing keys of different accounts
+are unrelated: a user who shares an account's viewing key, for example with
+an auditor or a watch-only service, keeps messages from its holder only by
+receiving them at addresses of another account.
+
+**Mailbox Servers.** A server never learns a network identity. It sees each
+Mailbox ID it holds and the number, size, and timing of the Envelopes
+deposited in and fetched from it. A Contact Mailbox lives as long as its
+address, and anyone who knows the address can compute its ID and server, so
+that server holds a long-lived traffic record for the address. Pairwise
+Mailbox IDs change every epoch and can be computed only by the two wallets
+and the responder's viewing key holders.
+
+**Linking addresses.** Diversified addresses of one wallet have unrelated
+Contact Mailboxes. A server can still link them if the wallet fetches them
+together, which is why fetches use separate sessions and schedules.
+
+**No opt-in signal.** Every address with an Orchard Receiver has a Contact
+Mailbox whether or not its wallet implements this ZIP, so a sender cannot
+tell whether its Envelope will be read.
+
+**The other wallet.** Envelopes do not authenticate their sender. An answer
+shows the sender that the recipient was online. Both wallets can fetch from
+the Pairwise Mailboxes of both directions, so each can see when the other's
+fetches cause its Envelopes to be deleted, and a wallet in Conversations with
+two addresses can compare them.
+
+**Network observers.** Privacy is bounded by the anonymity set of the Routing
+Binding. A wallet's entry point to the network sees its IP address but no
+Mailbox ID, server, or Zcash address.
+
+**Denial of service.** Anyone can deposit under any Mailbox ID, at the
+expense of the server's storage and the recipient's bandwidth.
+
+
+# Requirements
+
+- A sender holding only a recipient's Unified Address can deliver a message
+  with no prior contact, while the recipient is offline.
+- Unified Addresses and ZIP 316 are unchanged, and first contact needs no key
+  material beyond the recipient's existing Orchard keys.
+- A wallet can use many diversified addresses without a Mailbox Server, a
+  network observer, or a sender being able to link them.
+- No Mailbox Server or network observer learns the network identity of a
+  sender or recipient, and neither wallet learns the other's.
+- No party that sees a wallet's IP address is bound to that wallet's
+  addresses or mailboxes.
+- Two wallets can keep exchanging messages without a Mailbox Server
+  accumulating metadata under a long-lived identifier.
+- An Envelope reveals nothing about its content beyond its size.
+- The protocol does not depend on any one network or token.
+
+
+# Non-requirements
+
+- Sender authentication, guaranteed delivery, forward secrecy, and group
+  messaging.
+- Backup and recovery. Contact Mailboxes can be recomputed from the wallet's
+  addresses and viewing keys; Conversations cannot.
+
+
+# Specification
+
+## Notation
+
+$\mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}256}$ and $\mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}512}$
+[^protocol-blake2], $\mathsf{DiversifyHash^{Orchard}}$
+[^protocol-diversifyhash], $\mathsf{ToScalar^{Orchard}}$ [^protocol-orchardkeycomponents], $\mathsf{Sym}$ [^protocol-sym],
+$\mathsf{GroupHash}^{\mathbb{P}}$ [^protocol-grouphash],
+$\mathsf{repr}_{\mathbb{P}}$ and $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}$
+[^protocol-pallasandvesta], and $\mathsf{I2LEOSP}$ and $\mathsf{LEBS2OSP}$
+[^protocol-endian] are as defined in the Zcash Protocol Specification.
+
+- $\mathsf{PointBytes}(Q) = \mathsf{LEBS2OSP}_{256}(\mathsf{repr}_{\mathbb{P}}(Q))$.
+- $\mathsf{Scalar}(p, x) = \mathsf{ToScalar^{Orchard}}(\mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}512}(p, x))$.
+- $[b]$ is the one-byte string with value $b$.
+
+Integers are encoded little-endian. Times are in hours since the Unix epoch,
+rounded down.
+
+Throughout, $(\mathsf{d}, \mathsf{pk_d})$ is an Orchard Receiver with raw
+encoding $\mathsf{rcv}$, [^protocol-orchardaddrencoding] incoming viewing key
+$\mathsf{ivk}$, and
+$\mathsf{g_d} = \mathsf{DiversifyHash^{Orchard}}(\mathsf{d})$.
+
+## Envelopes
+
+| Field          | Type           | Description                         |
+|----------------|----------------|-------------------------------------|
+| `version`      | `byte`         | $1$                                 |
+| `ephemeralKey` | `byte[32]`     | $\mathsf{PointBytes}(\mathsf{epk})$ |
+| `ciphertext`   | `byte[N + 16]` | $N$ is 2048, 32768, or 262144       |
+
+The plaintext is:
+
+| Field          | Type                | Description                                   |
+|----------------|---------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
+| `seed`         | `byte[32]`          | Uniformly random                              |
+| `payload_type` | `u16`               | See [Payloads](#payloads)                     |
+| `flags`        | `byte`              | Bit 0: `ack_requested`                        |
+| `expiry_time`  | `u32`               | Time from which the Envelope is dropped       |
+| `fast_len`     | `byte`              | Length of `fast_reply`                        |
+| `fast_reply`   | `byte[fast_len]`    | See [Fast mode](#fast-mode); may be empty     |
+| `payload_len`  | `u32`               | Length of `payload`                           |
+| `payload`      | `byte[payload_len]` |                                               |
+| padding        | `byte[]`            | Zero bytes up to the smallest $N$ that fits   |
+
+Every Envelope belongs to a Conversation with secret $\kappa$, and is sent by
+its *initiator* ($\delta = 0$) or its *responder* ($\delta = 1$).
+$\mathsf{g_d}$, $\mathsf{pk_d}$, and $\mathsf{ivk}$ below are those of the
+responder's Receiver. With
+
+$\hspace{2em}\mathsf{esk} = \mathsf{Scalar}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WMsgEsk\_\_\_"}, \mathtt{seed}), \quad \mathsf{epk} = [\mathsf{esk}]\,\mathsf{g_d}$
+
+$\hspace{2em}\mathsf{K} = \mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}256}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WMsgPairK\_"}, \kappa \,||\, [\delta] \,||\, \mathtt{ephemeralKey})$
+
+the ciphertext is $\mathsf{Sym.Encrypt_K}$ of the plaintext.
+
+A *first Envelope* starts a Conversation. Its sender is the initiator, and
+
+$\hspace{2em}\kappa = \mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}256}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WMsgPairS\_"}, \mathsf{PointBytes}([\mathsf{esk}]\,\mathsf{pk_d}) \,||\, \mathtt{ephemeralKey})$
+
+which the responder computes from
+$[\mathsf{esk}]\,\mathsf{pk_d} = [\mathsf{ivk}]\,\mathsf{epk}$, as in Orchard
+note decryption.
+
+The recipient processes an Envelope only as a first Envelope to the Receiver
+whose Contact Mailbox it was fetched from, or in the Conversation and
+direction of the Pairwise Mailbox it was fetched from or of the `fast_reply`
+address it arrived at. It MUST drop the Envelope, with no behaviour that
+depends on which check failed, if:
+
+- `version` or the length is unknown;
+- decryption fails, the plaintext does not parse, or the padding is not zero;
+- $\mathtt{ephemeralKey} \neq \mathsf{PointBytes}([\mathsf{esk}]\,\mathsf{g_d})$;
+- `expiry_time` has been reached; or
+- it has already processed an Envelope with this `ephemeralKey`.
+
+It ignores the payload of an unknown `payload_type` and unknown bits of
+`flags`, which senders set to zero.
+
+## Payloads [payloads]
+
+| `payload_type` | Name            | `payload`                                     |
+|----------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|
+| $1$            | Ack             | `ephemeralKey` of the acknowledged Envelope   |
+| $2$            | Text            | UTF-8 text for display to the user            |
+| $3$            | Payment request | UTF-8 ZIP 321 URI [^zip-0321]                 |
+| $4$            | PCZT            | Serialized PCZT [^pczt]; format reference TBD |
+
+An Ack MUST NOT set `ack_requested`. Payloads MUST NOT carry spend authority,
+such as spending keys or ZIP 324 URIs. [^zip-0324]
+
+## Mailboxes
+
+A Mailbox ID is $\mathsf{PointBytes}(G) \,||\, \mathsf{PointBytes}(P)$, where
+$P = [a]\,G$ for a scalar $a$ that authorizes fetching. A derivation below
+that yields $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}$ for $G$ or $P$ defines no mailbox.
+
+The **Contact Mailbox** of a Receiver has
+
+$\hspace{2em}r = \mathsf{Scalar}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WMsgMbxOrc"}, \mathsf{rcv}), \quad G = [r]\,\mathsf{g_d}, \quad P = [r]\,\mathsf{pk_d}$
+
+so $a = \mathsf{ivk}$.
+
+The **Pairwise Mailbox** of a Conversation for direction $\delta$ and epoch
+$e$ has, with $m = \kappa \,||\, [\delta] \,||\, \mathsf{I2LEOSP}_{32}(e)$,
+
+$\hspace{2em}G = \mathsf{GroupHash}^{\mathbb{P}}(\texttt{"z.cash:WalletMsg-pair"}, m), \quad a = \mathsf{Scalar}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WMsgPairX\_"}, m), \quad P = [a]\,G$
+
+The epoch at time $t$ is $\mathsf{floor}(t / 168)$.
+
+A Server List entry is a 32-byte `server_id` and, for each network the server
+is on, an address in the format of that network's Routing Binding. The
+Mailbox Server of a Mailbox ID $\mathsf{id}$ is the entry with the smallest
+$\mathsf{BLAKE2b\text{-}256}(\texttt{"Zcash\_WMsgSrvSel"}, \mathtt{server\_id} \,||\, \mathsf{id})$,
+compared as a byte string.
+
+TODO: specify the Server List; see [Open issues](#open-issues).
+
+## Conversations
+
+A first Envelope is deposited in the Contact Mailbox of the Receiver it is
+encrypted to. In the Conversation it starts:
+
+- An Envelope is deposited in the Pairwise Mailbox of its sender's direction
+  and of the epoch in which it is deposited.
+- The responder fetches the Pairwise Mailboxes for $\delta = 0$ from the
+  moment it first sends an Envelope.
+- The initiator fetches the Pairwise Mailboxes for $\delta = 1$ for as long
+  as it wants an answer. It MUST NOT send another Envelope in the
+  Conversation until it has received one; until then, anything further it
+  sends is another first Envelope.
+- A wallet fetches the mailbox of the current epoch, and that of an ended
+  epoch until it has fetched it at least 24 hours after the epoch ended.
+
+Each Conversation costs the responder a fetch schedule, so a wallet SHOULD
+NOT answer a first Envelope, even with an Ack, without the user's approval.
+Either wallet MAY forget a Conversation at any time; the other is not told.
+
+## Mailbox Servers
+
+| Request | Fields                                                                  | Response                        |
+|---------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------|
+| Deposit | $[1]$, `mailbox_id`, an Envelope                                        | None                            |
+| Fetch   | $[2]$, `mailbox_id`, `after` (`u64`), `time` (`u32`), `sig` (`byte[64]`) | (`seq` (`u64`), `len` (`u32`), Envelope) triples |
+
+The server gives each deposited Envelope a nonzero `seq` greater than any it
+has ever given under that Mailbox ID. Fetch returns, in order, the Envelopes with
+`seq` greater than `after`, up to a size of the server's choosing, and allows
+the server to delete those with `seq` up to `after`. The server MAY also
+discard Envelopes after a retention period of its choosing.
+
+`sig` is a RedPallas signature [^protocol-reddsa] with generator $G$ in place
+of the fixed one, signing key $a$, and validating key $P$, over `server_id`
+followed by the request without `sig`. The wallet SHOULD make the signature's
+random input $T$ depend on $a$ as well as on fresh randomness, since a
+repeated or predictable $T$ reveals $a$.
+
+The server MUST drop a request, without responding, if it is malformed, including
+when either half of `mailbox_id` is not the encoding of a Pallas point other
+than $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}}$, or, for Fetch, if `time` is not within an hour of the server's clock or `sig`
+does not validate. It MUST NOT distinguish a mailbox it holds nothing for
+from an empty one.
+
+## Routing
+
+A Routing Binding carries requests to Mailbox Servers and responses back. It
+MUST:
+
+- hide the wallet's network identity from the server and from everyone but
+  the wallet's own entry point to the network;
+- keep requests and responses confidential and authentic between the wallet
+  and the server;
+- provide *sessions* such that neither the server nor a network observer can
+  tell whether two requests in different sessions come from one wallet.
+
+Its specification states the server address format, the framing of requests,
+responses, and Envelopes sent in fast mode, what a session is, and what each
+party can observe.
+
+A wallet MUST use a new session for each Deposit, and MUST NOT use one
+session for two Mailbox IDs. It MUST NOT bypass the anonymity network when it
+is unavailable.
+
+### Fast mode [fast-mode]
+
+A Routing Binding MAY define addresses at which a wallet can receive
+Envelopes directly for a limited time without revealing its network identity
+to the sender. `fast_reply`, if not empty, is:
+
+| Field         | Type     | Description                               |
+|---------------|----------|-------------------------------------------|
+| `network_id`  | `byte`   | Identifies the Routing Binding            |
+| `valid_until` | `u32`    | Time from which the address is not used   |
+| `address`     | `byte[]` | As specified by the Routing Binding       |
+
+A wallet MUST create a new address for each `fast_reply` and use it for
+nothing else, so that neither its host nor the other wallet can tie it to a
+Zcash address or to another `fast_reply`.
+
+A wallet that answers an Envelope with a `fast_reply` MAY, before
+`valid_until` and as well as depositing its answer, send the same Envelope to
+`address` from a session used for nothing else.
+
+## Wallet behaviour
+
+- Wallets SHOULD fetch each mailbox on its own randomized schedule,
+  independent of user actions and of their other mailboxes, and SHOULD set
+  `after` to the last `seq` they received, or to $0$.
+- Wallets SHOULD delay Acks, and deposits that are not part of an interactive
+  exchange, by a random amount, in particular relative to a related on-chain
+  broadcast. They SHOULD send an Ack only when `ack_requested` is set.
+- Wallets MUST NOT present a message as coming from a named party.
+- Wallets SHOULD NOT fetch the Contact Mailboxes of an account whose incoming
+  viewing key they have exported, and SHOULD give out addresses of another
+  account for messaging instead. If they do fetch them, they SHOULD tell the
+  user that the holder of the key can read and delete the account's messages
+  and send messages in its Conversations.
+
+
+# Rationale
+
+**Why reuse the Orchard keys?** Any address with an Orchard Receiver is
+already a public encryption key, so first contact needs nothing new. The cost
+is the power it gives incoming viewing key holders.
+
+**Why derive the mailbox instead of advertising it?** Advertising it would
+need a ZIP 316 Metadata Item, lengthen addresses, and allow one mailbox to be
+put in two addresses, linking them. Derivation gives every diversified
+address its own mailbox. In exchange, senders cannot tell whether a recipient
+reads messages, wallets have to agree on a Server List, and fetching has to
+be authorized by a key the wallet already has.
+
+**Why is a Mailbox ID a pair of points?** It lets a server verify knowledge
+of $\mathsf{ivk}$ without having been told anything by the recipient, and
+without the fetcher revealing its Receiver. Under the Decisional
+Diffie–Hellman assumption the pair cannot be linked to the Receiver or to
+the mailbox of another address with the same $\mathsf{ivk}$; neither can the
+signatures.
+
+**Why is $\mathsf{epk}$ checked?** For the reason given in ZIP 212:
+[^zip-0212] an Envelope encrypted to one address also decrypts under any
+other address with the same $\mathsf{ivk}$, so without the check a sender
+could deposit an Envelope made for one address in the mailbox of another and
+learn from a reaction that they belong to one wallet. The check also ties
+$\kappa$ to a single Receiver.
+
+**Why Conversations?** A Contact Mailbox gives its server a record of
+everything sent to an address. Pairwise Mailboxes move an ongoing exchange to
+identifiers that change weekly, and they give the recipient a way to answer
+without the sender disclosing an address. Shorter epochs would leak less but
+cost a returning wallet one fetch per missed epoch and Conversation.
+
+**Why is there no Delete request?** Deleting on the next fetch puts a random
+delay between reading an Envelope and its disappearance, which the sender in
+a Conversation can observe.
+
+**Why separate routing from mailboxes?** A party that stores messages for a
+wallet's address and also sees the wallet's IP address, as a Nym gateway
+named in an address would, can link the two. Here the server that stores
+Envelopes never sees an IP address, and the entry point that sees one never
+learns a Mailbox ID. It also means wallets on different networks can exchange
+messages, and the protocol outlives any one network.
+
+**Why fixed sizes?** Exact lengths would leak payload types.
+
+**Why no ZIP 324 payload?** A sender on this channel already holds the
+recipient's address and can pay it, and a ZIP 324 URI carries spend authority
+that every incoming viewing key holder could use.
+
+
+# Reference implementation
+
+None yet.
+
+
+# Open issues [open-issues]
+
+- The Server List: encoding, maintenance, distribution, authentication,
+  handling of changes, and whether one network is mandatory to implement. If
+  operators could choose their `server_id`, one could choose it so as to be
+  selected for a particular address.
+- Who runs Mailbox Servers and what pays for them; quotas, retention, and
+  whether Deposit should carry a payment or proof of work.
+- Whether an opt-in signal is needed after all.
+- Whether Conversations should add an ephemeral key exchange in their first
+  two Envelopes. That would give forward secrecy and shut out a viewing key
+  holder who only reads, though not one who answers a first Envelope before
+  the wallet does. First Envelopes cannot be protected without publishing a
+  separate messaging key, for which an address has no place.
+- Whether Fetch needs a way to skip large Envelopes.
+- Sapling-only recipients.
+- Payload types for FROST round messages, with their authentication, and for
+  off-chain note delivery.
+
+
+# Appendix A: Routing Bindings (non-normative)
+
+These sketches exist so that the protocol can be evaluated against real
+networks. Items marked TBD have to be resolved before either is normative.
+
+## Nym mixnet
+
+`network_id` $1$.
+
+- **Server address.** The 96-byte Nym client address [^nym-addressing] of a
+  client run by the server.
+- **Sessions.** A Nym client with fresh keys. Each has to register with an
+  entry gateway and hold bandwidth credentials; the cost and latency per
+  request, and who pays, are TBD.
+- **Framing.** A request is one Nym message. Fetch attaches reply SURBs
+  [^nym-surbs] for the response; how many, and how the server asks for more,
+  is TBD.
+- **Fast mode.** `address` is the 96-byte address of a client created for
+  the purpose, with an independently chosen gateway; an Envelope is one Nym
+  message. Its gateway holds messages while the client is offline, for
+  24 hours by default, [^nym-gateway-retention] which bounds `valid_until`.
+- **Observability.** A wallet's entry gateway sees its IP address and traffic
+  volume but not the destination. Mixing delays and
+  cover traffic hinder a global passive adversary. Larger Envelopes take more
+  packets.
+
+## Tor
+
+`network_id` $2$.
+
+- **Server address.** The 32-byte public key of a version 3 onion service.
+  [^tor-rend] The port is TBD.
+- **Sessions.** A connection over a circuit shared with no other session.
+- **Framing.** One request per connection, with request and response each
+  preceded by a `u32` length (TBD).
+- **Observability.** A wallet's guard sees its IP address and traffic timing.
+  Tor adds no delays or cover traffic, so a global passive adversary can
+  correlate a wallet's traffic with requests arriving at a server.
+
+

@@ -0,0 +1,597 @@ + ZIP: Unassigned + Title: Legacy Wallet Key-Derivation Behaviors for Fund Recovery + Owners: Darío Paz + Credits: Kris Nuttycombe + Oscar Pepper + Evan Branigan + Status: Draft + Category: Informational + Created: 2026-02-08 + License: MIT + Discussions-To: + Pull-Request: + + +# Terminology + +This document uses terminology from the Zcash Protocol Specification [^protocol], +BIP 32 [^bip-0032], BIP 39 [^bip-0039], BIP 44 [^bip-0044], ZIP 32 [^zip-0032] and +ZIP 316 [^zip-0316]. + +The terms "Mainnet" and "Testnet" in this document are to be interpreted as +defined in the Zcash Protocol Specification [^protocol-networks]. + +The terms below are to be interpreted as follows: + +Account index +: The index at the `account` level of a ZIP 32 or BIP 44 derivation path. + +Coin type +: The value at the `coin_type` level of a ZIP 32 or BIP 44 derivation path, as + registered in SLIP 44 [^slip-0044]. This is 133 for Mainnet and 1 for Testnet. + +Diversified address +: One of many addresses that a wallet derives from a single Sapling or Orchard + full viewing key, each with its own diversifier. One incoming viewing key + finds the funds of all diversified addresses of that key. + +Mnemonic phrase +: A sequence of words that encodes entropy, as specified in BIP 39 [^bip-0039]. + +BIP 39 seed +: The 64-byte value that the BIP 39 seed derivation function (PBKDF2) calculates + from a mnemonic phrase and a passphrase. + +Phrase entropy +: The bytes that a mnemonic phrase encodes. A wallet gets them when it decodes + the words of the phrase. + +Legacy HD seed +: The 32-byte seed that `zcashd` generated from system randomness and used for + Sapling key derivation, from v2.0.1 until the upgrade to v4.7.0. + +Mnemonic seed +: The name that `zcashd` v4.7.0 and later use for the BIP 39 seed of the wallet's + emergency recovery phrase. + +Legacy account +: The account with index `0x7FFFFFFF` under the mnemonic seed of a `zcashd` + wallet. It contains the addresses that the `getnewaddress` and + `z_getnewaddress` RPC methods return. + +Legacy derivation +: A key generation or key derivation behavior of an older wallet that a + recovery tool has to implement to find the funds of that wallet. + +Gap limit +: The number of consecutive unused indexes after which a recovery tool stops a + derivation sequence. + +The notation `m_Sapling` and `m_Orchard` is used as in ZIP 32 [^zip-0032] for the +Sapling and Orchard master keys. The notation `m` is the BIP 32 master key. An +apostrophe after an index identifies hardened derivation. + + +# Abstract + +Zcash wallets have used many strategies to generate and derive keys. A recovery +tool finds the funds of an old wallet only if it implements the strategy that +the wallet used. + +This ZIP describes the legacy behaviors that are important for fund recovery. It +specifies, for each wallet, the seed material, the derivation paths, the rules +that select the next index, and the procedure to recover funds. The first +version includes `zcashd`, Zecwallet Lite, and wallets that are based on the +`zcash_client_backend` and `zcash_client_sqlite` crates. + +Consensus rules are unchanged. The privacy implications apply to recovery tools: +recovery uses many viewing keys and many addresses for one user, which can +reveal to an observer that these addresses have one owner. + + +# Motivation + +Users can have seed material, wallet files, or partial backups that older +wallets made. Most recovery tools implement one scheme: a BIP 39 mnemonic +phrase, a BIP 39 seed, ZIP 32 derivation, and diversified addresses. Funds that +an older scheme created are invisible to such a tool. The user then concludes +that the funds are lost. + +Two examples: + +- A `zcashd` wallet from before v4.7.0 gets an emergency recovery phrase at the + upgrade. A different wallet that imports this phrase finds only the funds of + the unified accounts. The Sapling funds from before the upgrade are at other + paths, as are the funds at `getnewaddress` and `z_getnewaddress` addresses. +- Zecwallet Lite made a new spending authority each time the user asked for a + new Sapling address. A wallet that scans account 0 finds only the funds of the + first address. + +`zcashd` is deprecated, and Zecwallet Lite is unmaintained. The original +software becomes more difficult to run each year. A specification of these +behaviors lets implementers: + +- identify the recovery strategies that apply to a given wallet; +- write tools that recover funds independently of the original wallet software; +- recognize these patterns when they design a new wallet. + + +# Privacy Implications + +The implications below apply to software that implements the recovery +procedures in this document. + +- Recovery can use many viewing keys and many transparent addresses for one + user. A server that receives them (for example, a light wallet server that + answers transparent address queries) learns that the addresses have one owner. + Recovery tools need to keep such queries to a minimum. +- At the completion of recovery, the user frequently moves all found funds to + one new wallet. This transaction connects the transparent addresses on chain. It also + reveals the value that moves between pools. +- Recovered seed material, phrase entropy, and derived keys are as sensitive as + the original wallet. The legacy HD seed of a `zcashd` wallet has the same + entropy as its emergency recovery phrase: a person who gets one of them also + has the other. +- A viewing key for one Zecwallet Lite Sapling address reveals the funds of that + address only. Recovery uses one viewing key for each address. + + +# Requirements + +- An implementer can derive, from the seed material and this document alone, + each key that the documented wallet derived. +- The document identifies the funds that exist only in a wallet file, and the + backup that is necessary for those funds. +- The document identifies the wallet versions and products that each behavior + applies to. +- An implementer can do each procedure with independent software. + + +# Non-requirements + +- Wallet file formats (for example `wallet.dat` and the Zecwallet Lite wallet + file) are out of scope. The reference implementations parse these formats. +- The method that a recovery tool uses to move the recovered funds is out of + scope. +- New wallets are out of scope. The behaviors in this ZIP are for recovery only. + + +# Specification + +This ZIP is informational. Each subsection describes what a wallet did, then +what a recovery tool needs to do. + +In all derivation paths, `coin_type` is the coin type of the network of the +wallet. + +## `zcashd` + +### Summary of `zcashd` behavior + +The key generation of the `zcashd` wallet has three periods. The table gives the +source of new keys in each period. + +| Key type | Before v2.0.1 | v2.0.1 until v4.7.0 | v4.7.0 and later | +|-------------|---------------|---------------------|------------------| +| Transparent | Random | Random | Mnemonic seed | +| Sprout | Random | Random | Random | +| Sapling | Random | Legacy HD seed | Mnemonic seed | +| Orchard | None | None | Mnemonic seed | + +"Random" means that the wallet generated each key independently from system +randomness. Such a key exists only in the wallet file. + +- Transparent keys were random until v4.7.0. The wallet generated them ahead of + time and kept them in a keypool. +- Sprout spending keys were random in all versions. +- Sapling keys from v2.0.0 were random. Version 2.0.0 had Sapling as an + experimental Testnet feature. +- From v2.0.1, the wallet derived Sapling keys with ZIP 32 from the legacy HD + seed [^zcashd-2.0.1]. The wallet generated this seed directly from system + randomness. +- From v4.7.0, the wallet has an emergency recovery phrase. It derives all new + transparent, Sapling and Orchard keys from the mnemonic seed [^zcashd-4.7.0]. + +A wallet that the user made before v4.7.0 keeps all its old keys through each +upgrade. One `wallet.dat` file can contain keys from all three periods. + +### Seed material of `zcashd` + +#### Legacy HD seed + +From v2.0.1, `zcashd` generated an HD seed for each wallet that had none. This +occurred when `zcashd` loaded the wallet, or, for an encrypted wallet, when the +user first unlocked it. The seed is 32 bytes from the system random number +generator. `zcashd` gave these bytes, unmodified, to the ZIP 32 Sapling master +key generation. + +Before v4.7.0, the backup of this seed was the `wallet.dat` file or the +`z_exportwallet` file. + +#### Emergency recovery phrase and mnemonic seed + +`zcashd` v4.7.0 generates the emergency recovery phrase for each wallet that has +none. This occurs when `zcashd` loads the wallet, or, for an encrypted wallet, +when the user first unlocks it. The phrase is an English BIP 39 mnemonic phrase +of 24 words, which encodes 32 bytes of phrase entropy. + +The source of the phrase entropy depends on the wallet: + +- For a wallet with a legacy HD seed, the phrase entropy is the 32 bytes of the + legacy HD seed. The phrase is an encoding of that seed. +- For all other wallets, the phrase entropy is 32 bytes from the system random + number generator. + +`zcashd` then calculates the mnemonic seed, which is the BIP 39 seed of the +phrase with the empty passphrase. `zcashd` accepts the phrase only if the +mnemonic seed gives a valid unified spending key for account 0 and valid +transparent keys for the legacy account. For a rejected phrase: + +- in the random case, `zcashd` generates new entropy and tries again; +- in the legacy HD seed case, `zcashd` adds 1 (modulo 256) to the first byte of + the entropy and tries again, a maximum of 256 times. + +The probability of a rejected phrase is negligible. For almost all wallets with +a legacy HD seed, the phrase entropy is equal to that seed. + +Such a wallet has two seeds that come from one phrase: + +| Seed | How to get it from the phrase | Keys | +|----------------|-----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------| +| Legacy HD seed | Decode the words to the 32 bytes of phrase entropy | Sapling keys derived before the upgrade | +| Mnemonic seed | BIP 39 seed derivation, empty passphrase (64 bytes) | All keys derived after the upgrade | + +
+ +The legacy HD seed is the phrase entropy, which is outside the BIP 39 seed +derivation. A tool that calculates only the BIP 39 seed of the phrase finds only +the keys from after the v4.7.0 upgrade. + +After the upgrade, `zcashd` generates new addresses only when the user has +confirmed the backup of the phrase. The user gets the phrase from the +`z_exportwallet` file and confirms it with `zcashd-wallet-tool`. The option +`-walletrequirebackup=false` disables this requirement. + +### Derivation and address generation in `zcashd` + +#### Sapling keys from the legacy HD seed (v2.0.1 until v4.7.0) + +Each time the user ran `z_getnewaddress` for a Sapling address, the wallet +derived a new extended spending key from the legacy HD seed, at this path: + + m_Sapling / 32' / coin_type' / k' + +The index `k` comes from a counter in the wallet file (`saplingAccountCounter`). +The first value is 0, and each derivation adds 1. The wallet omitted an index +whose key it already had. + +The RPC method returned the default diversified address of that key. This was +the only address of the key that the wallet gave to the user. Each Sapling +address has its own spending authority, at its own ZIP 32 account index. + +#### Unified accounts from the mnemonic seed (v4.7.0 and later) + +`z_getnewaccount` makes accounts from the mnemonic seed with indexes 0, 1, 2, +and higher. Derivation follows ZIP 32 [^zip-0032] and ZIP 316 [^zip-0316]. +`z_getaddressforaccount` returns diversified unified addresses for an account. +The transparent receiver of a unified address has a BIP 44 address index that is +equal to the diversifier index of the unified address. + +#### Sapling addresses in the legacy account (v4.7.0 and later) + +Each time the user runs `z_getnewaddress` for a Sapling address, the wallet +derives a new extended spending key from the mnemonic seed, at this path: + + m_Sapling / 32' / coin_type' / 0x7FFFFFFF' / i' + +The last level is the `address_index` level that ZIP 32 permits below the +account level [^zip-0032-sapling-key-path]. `zcashd` uses hardened derivation +for it. + +The index `i` comes from a counter in the wallet file. The first value is 0, and +each derivation adds 1. The wallet omits an index whose key it already has. The +RPC method returns the default diversified address of the key. Each such address +has its own spending authority. + +Unified accounts have indexes that begin at 0. The account index `0x7FFFFFFF` +keeps the legacy keys apart from them. + +#### Transparent addresses in the legacy account (v4.7.0 and later) + +From v4.7.0, `getnewaddress` derives the key from the mnemonic seed with BIP 44, +on the external chain of the legacy account: + + m / 44' / coin_type' / 0x7FFFFFFF' / 0 / i + +The internal chain of the legacy account supplies the transparent change +addresses and the keypool keys: + + m / 44' / coin_type' / 0x7FFFFFFF' / 1 / i + +`zcashd` takes the addresses for miner rewards from the keypool. + +The wallet file has one counter for each chain. The first value is 0, and each +derivation adds 1. The wallet omits an index for which BIP 32 derivation fails. + +When v4.7.0 generates the mnemonic seed, it replaces the unused random keys in +the keypool with internal chain keys. Random keys that the wallet already gave +to the user remain in the wallet. + +#### Semantics of the legacy transparent pool + +`zcashd` treats all transparent funds outside the unified accounts as one pool. +This pool contains the funds at: + +- random keys from before v4.7.0; +- imported transparent keys; +- legacy account keys, on the external and the internal chain. + +An RPC method that spends from this pool (for example `sendtoaddress` or +`sendmany`) can select inputs from any of these addresses. It sends the change +to a new internal chain address. Funds that arrived at one address can be at a +different address later. A recovery tool needs to scan all keys of the +pool. + +TODO: confirm the exact list of RPC methods and the `ANY_TADDR` behavior of +`z_sendmany` against the `zcashd` source. + +### Recovery of `zcashd` funds + +#### Recovery from the emergency recovery phrase + +A recovery tool that has the emergency recovery phrase needs to do all the steps +below. The counters exist only in `wallet.dat`. For this reason, the tool +selects a gap limit for each step. + +1. Calculate the mnemonic seed: the BIP 39 seed of the phrase, with the empty + passphrase. +2. Unified accounts: for account indexes 0, 1, 2, and higher, derive the unified + full viewing key from the mnemonic seed. Scan for Sapling, Orchard and + transparent funds. +3. Legacy account, Sapling: for `i` = 0, 1, 2, and higher, derive the key at + `m_Sapling / 32' / coin_type' / 0x7FFFFFFF' / i'` from the mnemonic seed. Scan + with its viewing key. +4. Legacy account, transparent: for `i` = 0, 1, 2, and higher, derive the keys + at `m / 44' / coin_type' / 0x7FFFFFFF' / 0 / i` and + `m / 44' / coin_type' / 0x7FFFFFFF' / 1 / i` from the mnemonic seed. Find the + unspent outputs at their addresses. +5. Sapling keys from before the upgrade: decode the phrase to its 32 bytes of + phrase entropy. Use these bytes as the legacy HD seed. For `k` = 0, 1, 2, and + higher, derive the key at `m_Sapling / 32' / coin_type' / k'` from the legacy + HD seed. Scan with its viewing key. + +Step 5 finds funds only for a wallet that had a legacy HD seed, that is, a +wallet from v2.0.1 or later that the user updated to v4.7.0. + +In step 5, the first byte of the phrase entropy can be different from the first +byte of the legacy HD seed, as "Emergency recovery phrase and mnemonic seed" +specifies. The `getwalletinfo` RPC method gives the fingerprint of the legacy HD +seed (`legacy_seedfp`). A tool that has this fingerprint subtracts 1 (modulo +256) from the first byte, a maximum of 255 times, until the fingerprint of the +candidate seed is equal to it. + +#### Funds that need the wallet file + +These keys exist only in the wallet file: + +- all Sprout keys; +- transparent keys that the wallet generated before v4.7.0; +- Sapling keys that v2.0.0 generated on Testnet; +- keys that the user imported (for example with `importprivkey` or + `z_importkey`). + +Recovery of these funds needs the `wallet.dat` file, or the keys in a +`z_exportwallet` or `dumpwallet` file. The v4.7.0 release notes recommend that +users move funds from old addresses to newly generated addresses, to make the +phrase sufficient for all funds [^zcashd-4.7.0]. + +#### Recovery from a `wallet.dat` file + +A tool that has the `wallet.dat` file reads all keys directly, with their HD key +paths and seed fingerprints. This method recovers all funds of the wallet, +including the random keys. The reference implementation uses this method. + +### Open questions for `zcashd` + +- ZIP 32 gives v4.6.0 as the first version with Sapling addresses in the legacy + account [^zip-0032-sapling-key-path]. The release notes and the source give + v4.7.0. One of the two documents needs a correction. +- Recommend gap limits for steps 2 to 5. +- Describe in more detail the wallets that were encrypted at the time of each + upgrade. + +## Zecwallet Lite + +### Scope of the Zecwallet Lite behavior + +This section applies to the products that used the `zecwalletlitelib` light +client library [^zecwallet-light-cli]: + +- Zecwallet Lite for desktop; +- Zecwallet Lite for Android and iOS (`zecwallet-mobile`); +- the command-line client `zecwallet-light-cli`; +- forks of that library, for example `zwl-lib` [^zwl-lib]. + +Zecwallet FullNode was a user interface for the `zcashd` RPC interface. Its keys +follow the `zcashd` section above. + +### Summary of Zecwallet Lite behavior + +Each time the user asked for a new Sapling address, Zecwallet Lite derived a new +spending key at the next ZIP 32 account index. A wallet with $N$ Sapling +addresses has $N$ independent Sapling spending authorities, at account indexes +0 to $N - 1$. + +### Seed material of Zecwallet Lite + +Zecwallet Lite follows BIP 39: + +- A new wallet gets 32 bytes of entropy from the system random number generator. +- The wallet file contains these 32 bytes of entropy. +- The seed phrase that the user sees is the English BIP 39 mnemonic phrase of 24 + words for this entropy. +- The seed for key derivation is the BIP 39 seed (64 bytes) of that phrase, with + the empty passphrase. + +The phrase is sufficient to derive all keys that the wallet derived. + +### Derivation and address generation in Zecwallet Lite + +All paths below begin at the BIP 39 seed. In each rule, `n` is 0 for the first +key of a type. For each subsequent key, `n` is the highest existing index of +that type plus 1. + +| Key type | Path | Address | +|-------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------| +| Sapling | `m_Sapling / 32' / coin_type' / n'` | Default diversified address of the key | +| Transparent | `m / 44' / coin_type' / 0' / 0 / n` | P2PKH address of the key | +| Orchard | `m_Orchard / 32' / coin_type' / n'` | Orchard receiver of a unified address | + +- The Sapling rule is the legacy behavior. The path is a valid ZIP 32 account + path, in which the wallet used the account level as an address counter. +- The transparent rule is the external chain of BIP 44 account 0. +- The Orchard rule applies to the library versions that have Orchard. The + account level is an address counter here also. + +TODO: identify the first version of each product that has Orchard. + +Each key type has its own counter. + +The wallet has a gap rule (`GAP_RULE_UNUSED_ADDRESSES`) for Sapling and +transparent addresses. Its value is 5 on desktop and 0 on Android and iOS. On +desktop, when the wallet sees that one of the last 5 derived addresses of a type +was used, it derives more addresses of that type until 5 unused addresses follow +the last used address. On Android and iOS, the wallet +derives a new address only when the user asks for one. + +The wallet can also contain imported keys, which are independent of the seed. + +### Affected versions of Zecwallet Lite + +The Sapling behavior is in the last published version of `zecwallet-light-cli` +[^zecwallet-light-cli]. It is in the `zwl-lib` fork from v1.7.12 or earlier +[^zwl-lib], and in `zecwallet-mobile` up to version 1.8.8 or later +[^zingolib-2060]. All examined versions of the library have this behavior. +Recovery tools need to treat every version that offers more than one Sapling +address as affected. + +TODO: identify the first affected version of each product. + +### Recovery of Zecwallet Lite funds + +A recovery tool that has the seed phrase needs to do these steps: + +1. Calculate the BIP 39 seed of the phrase, with the empty passphrase. +2. Sapling: for `i` = 0, 1, 2, and higher, derive the extended spending key at + `m_Sapling / 32' / coin_type' / i'`. Scan with its viewing key. +3. Transparent: for `i` = 0, 1, 2, and higher, derive the key at + `m / 44' / coin_type' / 0' / 0 / i`. Find the unspent outputs at its address. +4. Orchard: for `i` = 0, 1, 2, and higher, derive the Orchard spending key at + `m_Orchard / 32' / coin_type' / i'`. Scan with its viewing key. + +The tool stops a sequence at the gap limit. A user can make an address and leave +it unused, which makes a gap limit of 1 or more necessary. The desktop gap rule +makes 5 the minimum for desktop wallets. Mobile users made addresses with a +button, in any quantity. The tool needs to let the user select a larger limit. + +Step 2 requires trial decryption of the full chain for each index. A tool can +use many viewing keys in one pass over the chain. + +
+ +When the mobile application restores a wallet from the seed phrase, it derives +the first addresses only, because the gap rule is 0 on Android and iOS. Funds at +Sapling addresses with a higher index are absent from the balance. These funds +are still spendable, and the procedure above finds them. + +Funds at imported keys need the wallet file or the imported keys. + +A current wallet that imports the phrase and scans account 0 finds the funds of +Sapling index 0, transparent index 0, and Orchard index 0. To find all funds, +the wallet needs to import each index `i` as a separate ZIP 32 account. + +## `zcash_client_backend` and `zcash_client_sqlite` + +Wallets that are based on the `zcash_client_backend` and `zcash_client_sqlite` +crates [^librustzcash] have used BIP 39 mnemonic phrases for key derivation in +all versions. Accounts follow ZIP 32, and addresses follow ZIP 316. + +The transparent addresses of these wallets get their indexes from three rules: + +- The default transparent address of an account is at child index 0 of the BIP + 44 external chain: `m / 44' / coin_type' / account' / 0 / 0`. +- Sequential BIP 44 derivation gives more transparent receivers, each at the + next address index. +- Unified address derivation, as ZIP 316 specifies, also gives transparent + receivers. Each one has a BIP 44 address index that is equal to the + diversifier index of the unified address. + +Diversifier indexes can have large gaps between them. A recovery tool needs a +transparent gap limit that allows for this. + +TODO: this section comes from review comments on the pull request. Verify it +against the source. Add the crate versions for each behavior, the ephemeral +(ZIP 320) address chain, and the gap limits that the crates use. + + +# Reference implementation + +- zexcavator [^zexcavator] is a wallet recovery tool. It will implement the + recovery procedures of this ZIP. +- The parser in `zecwallet-utils` [^zecwallet-utils] reads Zecwallet Lite wallet + files. It gets the entropy and the derived keys with their indexes. + + +# Open issues + +- Issue #1175 proposes that this ZIP describes all historic and present key + generation schemes, and replaces issue #503. More wallets need sections (for + example the mobile SDK wallets, YWallet, and hardware wallets). +- The open questions and TODO items in each wallet section. +- Decide if the recovery procedures use BCP 14 conformance key words. + + +# Acknowledgements + +Kris Nuttycombe opened issue #1175, which is the motivation for this ZIP. Kris +also supplied the details of the `zcashd` v4.7.0 upgrade and of the +`zcash_client_sqlite` behavior. +In Round Two of regular FROST, the Coordinator picks a message and sends it to
+each signer along with the commitments received in Round One. In Re-Randomized
+FROST, the Coordinator MUST additionally call $\mathtt{randomizer\_generate}()$
+and send the $\mathtt{randomizer\_seed}$ along with the message and the
+commitments. Each participant, upon receiving those values, MUST compute
+$\mathtt{randomizer}$ by calling $\mathtt{randomizer\_regenerate}()$ with the
+received $\mathtt{randomizer\_seed}$ and commitments.
+
+In Zcash, the message that needs to be signed is the SIGHASH transaction hash.
+This by itself does not convey enough information for the signers to decide
+whether they want to authorize the transaction or not. Therefore, in addition
+to the serialized transaction, more data (such as openings of value commitments,
+decryption of note ciphertexts, etc.) needs to be sent from the Coordinator to
+the signers. This SHOULD be done by sending a Partially Constructed Zcash Transaction
+[#zip-0374]_ over the same encrypted, authenticated channel. In order to sign,
+each signer MUST be satisfied that the transaction should be authorized, using
+the additional information provided in the PCZT where necessary. That information
+MUST be checked for consistency with the transaction and not trusted simply
+because the Coordinator is providing it.
+
+Each participant is a Signer in the sense of [#zip-0374-signer]_, and MUST
+perform the checks that ZIP 374 requires of a Signer before signing. In
+particular, each participant MUST compute the SIGHASH from its own copy of the
+PCZT, and MUST NOT sign any other message.
+
+Because the SIGHASH commits to the randomized validating key, which depends on
+the $\mathtt{randomizer}$, the Coordinator MUST complete Round One and derive
+the $\mathtt{randomizer}$ from its commitments before finalizing the PCZT.
+ZIP 374 describes the randomizer as chosen by the Constructor; for a FROST
+signing session, the Constructor is the Coordinator, and its choice is the
+derivation specified above.
